clips.when: Lesson opens and narration is switched on, or the listen button is pressed
clips.script: Welcome to the Cell Transport Lab. Every cell in your body is wrapped in a membrane, and that membrane is busy. Oxygen has to get in, waste has to get out, and water has to stay in balance. Over the next half hour, you're going to work out how it all happens, by experimenting, not just reading. First, a few quick questions, so I know where you're starting.

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to explain diffusion, osmosis and active transport, tell them apart, and use them to make sense of a real GCSE practical with potato. There's no pressure here. A wrong answer is useful, because it shows us exactly what to look at again.
Three quick questions. After each one, tell me how confident you are. This isn't a test, it's a starting point, and at the end I'll show you how far you've come.
Thanks. Keep hold of that starting point. Now let's go and meet our first process: diffusion.

This is the Diffusion Chamber. Every dot is a particle, and they're all moving randomly, bouncing off the walls and off each other. Nothing is pushing them anywhere. On the left there are lots of particles, and on the right, only a few. Before you open the divider, make a prediction. Which way will the overall movement go?

clips.when: Five seconds after the learner first opens the divider
clips.script: Watch carefully. Every single particle is moving randomly. Some cross to the right, and some cross to the left. But there are more particles on the left, so more of them cross from left to right than the other way round. That overall difference is called net movement. Net movement from a higher concentration to a lower concentration is diffusion. Notice that nobody told the particles where to go.

clips.when: Learner opens the 'Why is it passive?' prompt
clips.script: Diffusion is passive. The cell doesn't spend any energy on it. The particles move because of their own kinetic energy, the energy of their motion. Keep that idea separate from the energy cells get from respiration, because we'll need that difference later.

clips.when: First equilibrium reached; temperature slider unlocks
clips.script: Now try changing the temperature and running it again. Predict first. Will a warmer chamber reach equilibrium sooner, or later?

clips.when: A rerun at a higher temperature reaches equilibrium sooner than the previous run
clips.script: Did you spot that? At a higher temperature the particles have more kinetic energy, so they move faster and spread out sooner. The end point is the same, equal concentration on both sides. Only the speed has changed.

clips.when: Learner has run two starts with different concentration differences
clips.script: A steeper concentration gradient means a bigger difference between the particles leaving the crowded side and those arriving from the sparse side. So the net movement is faster at first, then it slows down as the gradient shrinks.

clips.when: Pore count changed after a completed run
clips.script: More pores mean more places for particles to cross at the same time, a bit like having more doors in a busy corridor. A larger membrane surface area speeds up diffusion. That's one reason the lungs have so many alveoli.

Look at the counters. Both sides are now roughly equal, and the net movement is zero. But the particles haven't stopped. Follow the highlighted one. It's still wandering, and particles are still crossing in both directions at about the same rate. That's dynamic equilibrium: lots of movement, but no net movement. The numbers wobble a little, because this model only has a small number of particles.

A common mix-up is thinking that particles want to spread out, or that they stop at equilibrium. Particles don't want anything, and they never stop moving. Spreading out is simply what random movement does to an uneven distribution.

In your body, oxygen diffuses from the air in the alveoli into the blood, because there's more oxygen in the lungs than in the blood. Carbon dioxide diffuses the other way. And urea, a waste made in liver cells, diffuses into the blood plasma, ready to be carried to the kidneys. None of these needs energy from respiration.

So, diffusion: the net movement of particles down a concentration gradient. It's passive, and it's affected by the steepness of the gradient, the temperature and the surface area. Next, a special case involving water.

Welcome to the Osmosis Chamber. This time there's a membrane in the middle, and it's partially permeable. The small, light blue water particles can pass through it. The larger solute particles can't. The left side is dilute, with only a few solute particles, and the right side is more concentrated. Predict which way the net movement of water will go, then press run.

clips.when: Six seconds after the first run starts
clips.script: Water is crossing in both directions. But the dilute side has proportionally more water particles, so more water crosses from the dilute side to the concentrated side than the other way. So osmosis is the net movement of water through a partially permeable membrane, from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution. It's diffusion, but only for water, so it's passive too.

clips.when: Level view switched on and the concentrated side rises
clips.script: The liquid level rises on the concentrated side. That's the result, not the cause. It rises because more water has crossed into that side.

clips.when: Both sides have equal solute and have run for five seconds
clips.script: Both sides now have the same concentration of solute. Water is still crossing the membrane in both directions, but at the same rate. So there's no net movement, and the level stops changing.
Now let's put a cell into different solutions. Choose a plant cell or an animal cell, choose the solution outside it, and predict what will happen before you watch.

The plant cell has taken in water by osmosis, because the solution outside is more dilute than the cell contents. It's become turgid, firm and swollen. The cell wall stops it bursting, and that firmness helps to support the plant's leaves and stems.
In a more concentrated solution, water has left the cell by osmosis, so the cell has become flaccid: soft and floppy. This is why a plant wilts when it doesn't have enough water.
An animal cell has no cell wall. In pure water it takes in water by osmosis, swells, and may burst. That's why the concentration of the fluid around our cells has to be carefully controlled.
In a stronger solution, water leaves the animal cell by osmosis, and the cell shrivels.

clips.when: Cell stabilises in an equal-concentration solution
clips.script: When the solution outside matches the inside of the cell, there's no net movement of water, and the cell stays the same size. Water is still moving in and out, just in equal amounts.

Two things to watch for. First, water moves in both directions. It's the net movement that goes from dilute to concentrated. Second, osmosis is only about water. In this model the solute stays put, and osmosis doesn't need energy from respiration.

So, osmosis: the net movement of water through a partially permeable membrane, from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution. Passive, and it explains why cells swell, shrink and stay firm. Next, something that does need energy.

So far, everything has moved down a concentration gradient. But sometimes a cell needs to take in a substance that's scarcer outside than inside. In this root hair cell, the ion concentration inside is higher than in the soil water. Diffusion would move ions out, not in. Predict: with the energy supply switched on, which way will the ions go overall?

clips.when: First carrier cycle completes, or learner clicks the protein
clips.script: Watch this carrier protein in the membrane. An ion binds to it. Then, using energy released by respiration, the protein changes shape and releases the ion on the other side. Each carrier is specific to particular substances, and it can only work so fast.

This is the key idea. Active transport needs energy from respiration, energy released from glucose in the cell, mainly in the mitochondria. That's not the same as the kinetic energy that makes particles move in diffusion. Passive movement comes from the particles themselves. Active transport is the cell doing work.

clips.when: Net uptake continues while inside concentration exceeds outside
clips.script: Look at the numbers. The inside already has more ions than the outside, and yet the count inside keeps rising. That's movement against the concentration gradient, from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated one. Diffusion could never do that.

clips.when: Energy at zero or inhibitor on for five seconds
clips.script: With the energy supply cut off, the carriers stop, and net uptake stops with them. The ions can't just slip across the membrane on their own. It's why plant roots struggle to take up minerals in waterlogged soil, where the shortage of oxygen slows respiration.

clips.when: Rate stops increasing as energy is raised
clips.script: More energy helped at first, but now the rate has levelled off. There's only a limited number of carrier proteins, and each one can only work so fast. Try adding more carriers and see what changes.

Two places this matters. Root hair cells take up mineral ions, such as nitrate, from the soil, even when the soil water contains a lower concentration of them. And in the small intestine, glucose is absorbed into the blood by active transport when there's less glucose in the gut than in the blood, so that none is wasted. Cells that do lots of active transport tend to have lots of mitochondria. Can you see why?
Active transport isn't just fast diffusion. It can move substances against the concentration gradient, it needs carrier proteins, and it needs energy from respiration.
So, active transport: moving substances against the concentration gradient, using carrier proteins and energy from respiration. Now let's bring all three together.
Time to pull it all together. Sort these statements into diffusion, osmosis and active transport. Some of them belong to more than one. Take your time.

clips.when: An energy statement is misplaced twice
clips.script: Think about energy from respiration. Which of these three processes needs the cell to spend it, and which two don't?

clips.when: A water-only statement is misplaced twice
clips.script: Ask yourself: which process is only ever about water? And does that process need a partially permeable membrane?

Well sorted. The big picture: diffusion and osmosis are both passive. Active transport is the odd one out. It needs energy from respiration, and it can move substances against the concentration gradient.

This is Required Practical Three. You're going to investigate how potato tissue changes in mass when it's placed in different concentrations of sugar solution. You'll plan it, run it, and then analyse the results. One reminder: the results in this lab are simulated. They're designed to be realistic, but they're not from a real experiment.
Choose your variables. What are you going to change? What are you going to measure? And what must stay the same, to keep the test fair?

Cut your potato cylinders to the same length and diameter, blot them dry, and measure the starting mass of each. Why blot? Liquid on the surface would add extra mass. And take care with the cork borer, because it's sharp.

Set up your tubes, each with the same volume of solution at a different concentration. Include distilled water, which is a concentration of zero. Leave them for the same length of time, at the same temperature.
Why use percentage change, rather than just the change in grams? Because the cylinders don't all start with exactly the same mass. A percentage lets us compare them fairly.
Percentage change in mass is the final mass minus the initial mass, divided by the initial mass, then multiplied by one hundred. If your answer is negative, the potato has lost mass.
Here are your results, and remember, they're simulated. Before you calculate anything, look for the pattern. Where does the mass go up, and where does it go down?
Now plot concentration on the horizontal axis, and mean percentage change in mass on the vertical axis. Then draw a smooth line of best fit through your points. Not dot to dot.

clips.when: Learner draws or confirms a best-fit curve
clips.script: Where does your line cross zero? With this data, it should be somewhere between zero point four and zero point six moles per decimetre cubed. At that concentration there's no net movement of water, which means the solution outside is about the same concentration as the inside of the potato cells. Water is still moving in and out. It's just balanced.
To write your conclusion, first describe the pattern, using numbers from your results. Then explain it using osmosis. Say which way the water moved, and why.

One of these results doesn't fit the trend. Is it an anomaly? Think about what might have gone wrong, perhaps uneven blotting, and what you could do about it, such as repeating the test and calculating a mean.

clips.when: Results generated with poorly chosen control variables
clips.script: Your results are quite scattered. Check your control variables. Were the volume, the time, the temperature and the size of the cylinders all the same? Anything left uncontrolled adds error.

Finally, evaluate your method. How could you make the results more reliable, and more precise? Think about repeats, a narrower range of concentrations around the crossing point, and a more sensitive balance.

This is your final assessment: eight questions, twenty-one marks. Read each question carefully, look at the command word, and use the number of marks as a guide to how many points to make. You'll see a mark scheme after each answer. Good luck.

clips.when: Learner opens the command words tip
clips.script: A quick tip on command words. 'Describe' means say what happens. 'Explain' means say why, using the science. 'Calculate' means show your working.

clips.when: Learner presses listen after a full-marks answer
clips.script: Well done. That's a clear answer, and you've used the key terms well.

clips.when: Learner presses listen after a partial-marks answer
clips.script: Close. You've got part of it. Compare your answer with the mark scheme and see which point is missing.

clips.when: Learner presses listen after a zero-marks answer
clips.script: Not quite this time. Read the explanation, and you can go back to the relevant simulation to see it in action.

clips.when: Final score is 80 per cent or above
clips.script: That's a very strong performance. You can explain all three processes, tell them apart, and apply them to a practical. Well done.

clips.when: Final score between 50 and 79 per cent
clips.script: A solid effort, and you've clearly built some strong foundations. There are a few areas to tighten up, and the breakdown below will show you where.
This topic takes a bit of time to settle, so don't be discouraged. Use the breakdown below to choose one area, replay its simulation, and then try the questions again.

clips.when: Learner presses listen on the diffusion revisit card
clips.script: For diffusion, go back to the chamber and focus on three things: random movement versus net movement, what happens at equilibrium, and the three factors that change the rate.

clips.when: Learner presses listen on the osmosis revisit card
clips.script: For osmosis, focus on the direction of net water movement, the words dilute and concentrated, and what happens to plant and animal cells in different solutions.

clips.when: Learner presses listen on the active transport revisit card
clips.script: For active transport, focus on what makes it different: the direction relative to the gradient, the carrier proteins, and the energy from respiration.

clips.when: Learner presses listen on the practical revisit card
clips.script: For the practical, rehearse the percentage change calculation, the variables, and how to read the point where the graph crosses zero.

clips.when: Learner opens the 'then and now' comparison
clips.script: Here's where you started, and here's where you are now. Look at the topics where the bars have moved the most. That's real progress.

To finish: diffusion and osmosis are passive, and move substances down a concentration gradient. Active transport uses energy from respiration to move substances against it. Membranes are partially permeable, and cells use all three processes to keep themselves working. Thanks for working through the lab.
